newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-Heineken mauled as Europe beer sales go flat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Heineken mauled as Europe beer sales go flat.

text.p: Investors savaged Heineken shares on Friday after disappointing first half results and a shock profit warning from the Dutch brewing giant prompted analysts to downgrade their estimates.

The group posted a six percent rise in first half 1996 net profit to 297 million guilders ($175.2 million), and warned that full-year net would be "somewhat" lower than 1995's 664 million guilders, blaming stagnant European beer markets.
Analysts had expected first half net profit of between 308 and 322 million guilders.
Heineken shares plunged over 50 guilders, or almost 14 percent, to a low of 312.00 guilders, before bouncing back to close down 40.20 guilders at 322.50.

Speaking at a news conference to present the results, Chairman Karel Vuursteen added to investors' woes by warning that double digit net profit growth for the group over the next three years could not be guaranteed.
"Within this integration phase it's very difficult to give a prediction, but over the next three years I don't think you can count on double digit net profit growth," he said.
He said the main problem dogging the group was that there would be no more growth in European beer markets, which would lead to increasing pressure on margins.
In 1995, Heineken beer sales in Europe accounted for almost half of total worldwide sales.

Vuursteen said recent acquisitions there, including the purchase of the Fischer Group in France in February, would take three years to contribute to net profit. He cited time needed to integrate distribution systems, brand portfolios and personnel.

"Although many beer markets -- mainly in Europe -- are saturated, we believe that we have to invest in them in order to build further for the sustainable profit growth of such a large part of our activities," Vuursteen added.
A number of analysts cut their own profit estimates following the group's pessimistic expectations.
Marius Andre, analyst at Amstgeld, said he would be cutting his full year 1996 net profit forecast to 650 million guilders from 750 million, versus the 1995 result of 664 million.
Dealers expected the stock to drop up to 20 guilders further on Monday as analysts digested comments from the company's presentation, and investors watched weekend press comment.

"It's possible if there are a lot of news items tomorrow that there will be more selling pressure early next week," said one share trader. "We think another 20 guilder fall on Monday is possible, unfortunately."
The results prompted frenzied dealing in Heineken stock with over 3.7 million shares changing hands on Friday against the usual 200,000 to 400,000.

Vuursteen said fine summer weather in 1995 meant sales volume in Europe appeared lower this year. He added cost increases in these markets could not be fully recovered through selling prices and the standard beer sector in particular was under pressure.

But this would be partly offset by a rise in exports and activities outside Europe. Sales in the Asia Pacific region showed a clear 16 percent rise over the six-month period to 690 million guilders from 593 million in the same 1995 period.
"This is particularly due to the higher sales in Indonesia and Vietnam, as well as the increased exports to China and Taiwan," Heineken said in a statement.
Exports to the U.S. also rose. Sales volume of exports there grew by a "satisfactory" 10 percent, Vuursteen said.

Heineken posted a 20.1 percent increase in group turnover to 5.92 billion guilders, and a 7.7 percent increase in trading profit to 464 million. Net profit per share rose to 5.92 guilders from 5.59 in the same year ago period.
The group announced an unchanged interim dividend of 1.50 guilders per share.
